div.p: Stella Kramer’s 1979 Vol. 2 edition of STELAZINE is a nonlinear compilation of Seattle punk scene goings-on, conveyed through a variety of interviews (conducted by Kramer herself), prose snippets, absurd poetry, and collage-esque photography and graphic layouts. Kramer is a local punk-scene legend and Pulitzer Prize-winning photo-journalist, who first had thoughts of developing a published zine after moving to Seattle in 1976 and becoming a part of the then-small punk-scene through informally writing reviews of local shows. It is through STELAZINE that Kramer blossomed the niche-punk and alternative scene of Seattle into the iconic focal point of music it is today.

This digital edition of Kramer’s STELAZINE hopes to make the zine more accessible to those who want to experience Kramer’s work. Previously, this was only accessible in print. We hope that by digitizing this physical media, it breathes new life into the work and words that were published almost 50 years ago. The content, interviews, and art contained in the zine open a door to the Seattle punk scene as it was in the 70s. These never-before-seen interviews with Poly Styrene (of X-Ray Spex) and Paul Simonon (The Clash) offer unique and interesting takes on not only their music, but the Seattle music scene—all of which would be lost to time without this zine. While it is difficult to digitally represent a zine that was not created with digitization in mind, we hope that the work we do here will incentivize people to perhaps go down to the Special Collections themselves to take a look at this zine and the many other amazing works that they house.

This zine includes quite a few spelling errors, which we elected to correct as an editorial team. We decided that the errors were not necessary to include in our digitized zine, and the integrity of the text is still retained with the corrections. We also elected to censor racial slurs by keeping the first letter and replacing the rest with asterisks. It may have been acceptable to type out the full word when this zine was published in the 70s, but the 2026 editing team did not feel comfortable keeping those uncensored slurs in our edition. The text still comes across in the same way with this censorship, and no readability is lost.

div.p: It took three days of massive telephoning. First to Epic Records in New York. Then to LA. Then to Vancouver. But I was determined to see them and talk to them. I finally connected with road manager Johnny Green in Vancouver, and after countless phone calls to their hotel, I found Caroline Coon. It wasn’t until the day of the show that things were arranged, but it was worth it. A lesson for all: Go directly to the band. I was allowed backstage after the show and waited around talking. Finally I was ushered into a small dressing room to talk to Paul. I entered, after stepping over Joe, Mick, and Topper, who were being interviewed by some asshole from the straight press. Paul was sitting on a leopard-covered couch in the corner, all in black. Wearing sunglasses. He intimidated me at first, as I sat on the floor next to him. But as the interview went on I relaxed and so did he. Too bad we were cut off just as we started to relax. So read on. This is a report about the Clash’s first gig in North America. All the way from January to you.

S: What did you think of the show? PAUL: It’s alright. It’s okay. We weren’t too bad for a first one, ‘cause usually we’re a bit rusty. We never played Canada or America before, so it’s pretty new. S: How do you prepare for a show, because you play really hard. You seem to expend all of your energy… PAUL: I dunno. Sometimes, it depends… what we’ve been doing the last couple of days is swimming. We had a game of football with the local kids ‘round here. S: I hear you’re good. PAUL: Yeah, we’re alright. We don’t overdo it–like drugs. I don’t have enough time for that. Makes me sleepy, anyway. So we don’t go in for all that. S: What are you thinking about when you are on stage? The song you’re playing? PAUL: What the next chord is! (Laughter) S: Do you notice the crowd alot? PAUL: Yeah, quite a lot. It’s pretty hard not to. S: Some people get so involved with the music, that they don’t see the crowd… lights in their eyes and all… PAUL: I dunno. I look at both. I gotta look down at what I’m playing anyhow, ‘cause I might hit the wrong note. It’s good fun though. S: You looked like you were having a really good time. PAUL: It’s alright. S: Do you improvise? PAUL: Yeah, sometimes. Sometimes I have to ‘cause I can’t remember the rest… But seriously. Sometimes I do, you know just to change it around a bit. S: Caroline said you don’t get much airplay in England PAUL: Not much. We had a terrible time trying to get airplay and all that. But everybody would buy our records, but there’d be no airplay. But since our last album came out it’s increased sligh-tly. S: Do you tour alot in England? PAUL: Quite alot, yeah. S: So that’s how people hear your music? PAUL: Yeah. We’re sort of like tops in England. S: You must get interviewed alot. PAUL: Yeah, quite alot. S: Do you like it? PAUL: I don’t mind. I quite enjoy it sometimes. I think it’s alright. It sort of makes you re-examine your beliefs on things. All sorts of things, you know. S: Caroline said you wanted opening bands to be female… PAUL: Yeah S: Is that with all the US gigs? PAUL: I don’t know. Not all of them, don’t think. But as many as possible. It’s good for a change. Usually people see just blokes getting up on stage all the time. If there’s girls getting up it makes a change, and it’s like… it’s pretty good ‘cause it encourages other girls to be in groups, and there ain’t really enough girls in groups these days it seems. S: It’s true. Are you going to get a chance to see the country? PAUL: We spent the last three days here. Walked around and like checked the place out. S: Never been here before? PAUL: No, never. And generally all the other shows we’ve got ‘round the country we’ll have a couple of days off. Not actually off, ‘cause we’ll have interviews to do. There’ll be an hour off here or there, so we’ll get out as much as possible and have a look around. S: Is it hard keeping contact with your audience? PAUL: It’s not hard at all. Just get out of your room and walk down the street, you know. That’s what I do. That’s what we all do, even when we’re back in London. People come up to us and talk to us. I quite enjoy that. It’s like having lots of friends. S: People aren’t afraid to approach you? PAUL: I don’t know. Sometimes and sometimes not. It’s all down to the actual person and how much they want to meet you, I suppose. S: Did you organize the tour? Or how much was it organized by the record company? PAUL: They sort of like… we decided where to play. Actually Caroline and an agency decided where to play. We can say we don’t want to play there, or whatever, but we never say that anyway… It’s the record company that at the moment puts up the money for us to tour; to have Bo Diddley on the tour. S: They determine how much the tickets cost? PAUL: To a certain extent..not too much. At the moment, because it’s the first tour that we’ve done, I suppose. They-’re generally smaller places we’re playing, and not too many people know about us, so the money we have to charge on the door (‘cause we have to pay for the road crew, lights, the PA…) on the next tour it will probably be more self-supporting, where with this tour CBS is paying quite alot. S: Do you find it different than you expected working with a record company? You’ve done two albums now, and as far as bands go, you’re in a more comfortable position… PAUL: Well, not really. We have alot of fights with the record company. There’s nothing you can do about it really, you just keep fighting. If you sign to a small record company… If we signed to a small record company we probably wouldn’t be here now, and probably half of the people in Britain and here and wherever wouldn’t have heard our records… It’s a choice. We never wanted to be a small or cult band. We wanted to be on top, you know? S: You’re new record has things which stick out more than on the first album. PAUL: Yeah, I dunno. I think it’s got it in the first album as well, except you can’t hear it too well., ‘cause of the way it was recorded. Whereas now it sounds alot clearer. There’s more depth in the record, so you can hear more in it. S: Are you still learning how to record? I assume with the second album you went into a good studio… PAUL: Well, no. We went into a studio that was as good as the first one we went into, except there are certain things you can do with microphones, and the type of cabinet–amplifier you use. When we recorded the first album we just had microphones up against each amplifier, and played it, and that was it. Whereas on the second album we had microphones up against the amps as well as two microphones at the end of the big room… so it’s got ambiance. S: Do you like recording? PAUL: It’s alright. It’s not bad. It’s a bit boring sometimes. S: Do you like touring? PAUL: Yeah, it’s pretty good fun, ‘cause you go to alot of different places. S: Do you get tired of playing the same songs over and over again? PAUL: No. They always seem to be a bit different. S: Do you rehearse alot? PAUL: Generally quite alot. It depends if we need to. S: Even though you have alot of fans, and your album is doing well, do you still have problems with rehearsal studios? I mean alot of bands can’t find studios, and if they do people don’t want them to play loud… PAUL: We did when we first started. But when we signed… joined up with Bernie Rhodes, our old manager, he got a rehearsal studio together for us. It was our own one so we could rehearse and be as loud as possible. Whereas lately we got rid of him and we’ve had problems getting a hold of rehearsal halls. S: Do you consider the band the same as it’s been all along? PAUL: Yeah. It’s just we can play better now. S: That must be a good feeling. PAUL: Yeah, it’s pretty good. [Pause while Topper gets a light for a cigarette] S: What kind of directions are you looking to take with the band? I understand you want to come back and tour in June. PAUL: Yeah, do a larger one. This is a small one really; just to see how it goes, I suppose. S: Do you want to go to, say, Japan? PAUL: Yeah. We’d like to go everywhere… As much as possible. We never really wanted to be stuck in London all the time. We all wanted to play everywhere. S: How much chance do you think there is for your music to get on the radio? In London the charts are so much different than they are here. Here it’s real disappointing. PAUL: Someday it’s bound to. Probably when we give up they’ll start playing it When we decide to do something else. S: What kind of music do you listen to? PAUL: Umm… sort of anything really. But generally I listen to old stuff like rockabilly and like Bo Diddley and Little Richard, and stuff like that. I like that a lot. And reggae, you know. S: Did you find it hard to listen to the ba-ss? PAUL: First I did. First six months it was really difficult. Then after awhile I played along with records and it got easier and easier. S: You just learned off of records? You didn’t take lessons? PAUL: No, not proper lessons. S: What made you decide to play bass? PAUL: Umm….. ‘Cause it’s easier to learn. It’s the quickest one you can learn. You can just strum a note and after awhile when you get better you can start to do little tunes. S: What kind of bass do you play? PAUL: Fender. It’s generally the most reliable. S: Are there alot of bands in England still forming; alot of bands still popping up, or has it leveled out? PAUL: It’s sort of leveled out a bit, but there are still new bands coming up here and there. S: Younger bands? PAUL: Who? S: Younger bands? PAUL: I thought you said yoga bands….. (Laughter) S: Younger. Like 15, 16…. PAUL: It sort of varies, you know. There’s that sort of younger….really younger groups, and then sort of older groups. It’s sort of even out, but there are still groups forming. S: Do you think it was easier for you..I don’t know how much you know about what goes on in the US, but most bands, especially bands on the east coast have trouble getting signed. It seemed that British bands had an easier time getting signed after awhile. CONTINUED ON PAGE 4

lg.l: New York, New York,......n.y. A city tingling in the cold. This city
never sticks. Winds creating a tunnel underneath the skyscrapers. At
times it hurts to breathe.
Watching Japanese television. Comedy shows from Japan Everything
with a wash of rice paper. Colors:from red to green:yellows into blue.
Calligraphy in sound and motion. Asian faces. Strange language. Who
knows what they are saying? Is this Tokyo?
Frantic humor/split images. Mass produced faces we can laugh at It
all comes back to me.........
Late night blue television. Tuning in for a quick fuck on the motor-
cycle.
We stay across from the Chelsea Hotel, in a loft with a great view of
watertowers. Fire escapes zig-zagging across the landscape.
I see the city through vertical lines. Cold metal slashing through
the cityscape. And people. Crazies in the all-night Have-a-Donut. Shop-
ping bags and twilight chatter. Sirens cutting holes in my brain.
A city always on the move. So many people you want to scream at times.
Prality comes in flashcubes of consciousness. You couldn't hold your
breath if you tried.......
Whispers drill holes in the midnight air. People in doorways eager
to talk. New York is the only place in the world were you can fall in
love with mannequins, he said.
Invisible people crowd corners. Datapanik in the year sero......
Subway stations deserted, like empty cages in a long forgotten zoo. The
crush of bodies during the days leaves you gasping for air. Everywhere
is the grasp for air....
This is what we saw.

div.p: There are three established clubs in the city:CBGB's, Max's, and Hurrah All week music. Admission is $4 to $6 depending on the day. Count on seeing anyone. It's the crowd that can sway your feelings. CB's is overrun with tourists eager for a glimpse of "new wave". You can't get out of your seat so where's the fun? Max's is better, although the sound isn't as good. Th- ere's a coldness about it to me. Hur- rah's is highly considered by people in the city. Getting better. Then there are the week-end clubs... Mudd Club, Club 57, Club Hollywood... Studio 10 and sometimes Trax. Studio 10 is a Yippie club in the west Vill- age. Club 57 is gaining prominence--- strong shows, good atmosphere and go- od fun. Admission is $4. One of the places to go to. Mudd Club is the most highly prais- ed. With acoustics rumored as being designed by the one and only Eno--- it is new and rising fast. Set in the Soho area it provides weekend entert- ainment of the most novel kind. Cons- tant choices.

Clubs advertize in the newspapers: Village Voice and Shoh Weekly. Other- wise you see wall posters. few bands print posters. New bands never do. We in Seattle have relied on wall posters like a great wall of informa¬ tion. But we have not had media acce- ptance. The price you pay for being a provincial city... Poster artwork runs the gamut from imaginative to boring. Too few of the former, too much of the latter. Opinions are worn on lapels in this city. Store bought, profuse. Why make them when you can buy them? The star- kest difference here is the accepti- bility of new wave. You can hang out in the East Villa- ge: Manic Panic (and talk to Snooky).. Trash & Vaudeville, Defiant pose... Or to the West Village and the Bowery¬ Next Empire and Revenge, Bookstores.. Record stores—the best being Village Oldies, where you can hear reggae on the radio, and any band you care to on the stereo. Even clothing if you're just in from the 'burbs.... Visit Punk Mag or the Rocker. Find

book stores full of fanzines. It's all here. A decent selection of local fanzin- es (besides the big two). Esther too eclectic, or too "in scene". The best are "Beat It" and "No"-the latter be ing crammed with the impact of eight million images, impact, writing and ? Find it. Lesser interesting ones inc- lude: the in-joke "Skull Damage" for affecionados exclusively; "Smegma'-- xerox and fun, and "2+2= 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 or 7 or 8 or 9" -done by Susan Springfield of the Erasers. As bori- ing as her band and as trite. Everyone wears black leather. Youre either punk or pop. Take it as you like. Lots of clothes for the clothes conscious. Lots of celebrities. Like most towns the people are spl- it. A and B lists of bands depend on who you're talking to. Too many imit- ations: of Patti, of the Heads, of our boys from OHIO. Some are fun. The au- diences are made up of old-timers, those who are or have been in bands. A few wide-eyed kids figuring they've stumbled onto something BIG. Then th-

ere are the tourists. Lots of bands are working on relea sing vinyl It helps the CB's puts out albums (the next one should be on the racks soon, and is worth picking up-ED.) People from established ban- ds will produce newer bands. It's im- pressive. There is a third generation gaining strength in the club scene. Bands who have watched the older ones form and are now attempting to avoid the same pitfalls. Knowledge is passed on. Visions continue to expand. Younger people on the way up..... Commercially New York is a pop town Witness the strength of Blondie, everyone's role model. But equally as strong is the knowledge of their decision and desire for money. The musicians continue to be accessable, and running into one can bring you into contact with another. New York, once the progeniter of radio stations has for the most part fallen into the disco pool. WNEW-AM : is now MOR. WNEW-FM, the first to give new wave a listen (because of well wo-

div.p: I wanted to interview Laura after hearing Student Teachers at CBGB's, and being impressed with her drumm- ing. Laura is a stand-out destined to make a name for herself. The interview was conducted at an apartment in Manhattan which Laura shares with Jimmy "The Housepainter Destri. We talked in the living room/bedroom, amid a ringing telepho- ne and Laura's sister. The one window on the room had a teriffic view of the city.......
S:How long have you been playing drums?
L:A year.
S:That's all?

L:Year, only a year. I took lessons for about four or five months and then I stopped. We started playing alot more, having alot of gigs. It taes money, so I never got around to picking up lessons again. So I took them for a few months, then just played along by myself, and watched other drummers, and picked up tips from friends of mine. I still have alot to learn.
S:How old are you?
L:17. We're a very young band.
S:I could tell.
L:I just turned 17 in December.
S:Were you instrumental in forming the band?

L:Yeah, well sort of. It all started with my keyboard player,Bill, my bass player and myslef who hada band at one time. But it was just an idea. I didn't play drums at the time, and she hadn't played bass, but we liked the idea of getting a band together.. We talked about it for about a year.. Then my keyboard player became very good friends with the singer, David. David said he had this guitarist fri- end, and brought him along. We had a photo session evenbefore we rehearsed, 'cause we all liked the way the other looked.
S:What's the name of your guitarist?

L:Phillip Shelley. We had this photo session... We knew nothing! Wewere just forming this band. Nobody knew what they wanted to do. We finally got our first rehearsal together. Slowly things started getting along, and we played our first gig at my high school.
S:Which one?

L:It's Friend's Seminary on E. 16th.. It's a private H.S. A joke, but we played a concert just to get the feel of playing in front of people. Our friends The Blessed came to see us ...They liked us, and were playing the next Sunday as Max's and said: "Why don't you open for us?" So we went to Max's (we knew the booking agent), and said:"Why don'cha let us do this?" She said fine. We didn't get billed or anything. It was like an audition for the club. They really liked us so we got another gig there a couple of weeks later. It st- arted like that. It was slow at first at the beginning, but then we found ouselves playing three or four gigs a month. Things star- ted going very fast. Then we had a gig at Max's. Bill came up and said, Jimmy Destri wants to take us into the studio. What do you think?" I said sure. We were all really excited. He came to lots of rehearsals and went over the songs, & we recorded in the middle of last July. Recorded our single, which isn't out yet,but should be soon.
S:What songs?
L:"Christmas Weather" and "The Quake"
S:"The Quake" seems to be a popular song.
L:Yeah, that's the one Bill and I wr -ite. The major songwriters are Bill & Phillip, which is strange, 'cause th- ey write in completely differnt ways
S:Was that your drumkit you used at CB's?
L:No.It was Jane's of the Erasers. It is an incredible drum kit. A vintage Pearl.
S:It was miked well.
JD:Thank you.

S:Yeah, my friend really liked the
sound of the tom-toms.
JD:Thanks.
L:It's a beutiful set. Her boyfriend bought it for her.
S:We should all be so lucky.
L:Yeah, we shoud have.....
JD:Boyfriends who buy drum sets!
S:DO you have your own kit?

L:Sort of. I'm loosing it rapidly. I bought a couple of drums from the Mu- mps drummer. Used drums 'cause I had no money. I bought a snare and two toms and a bass drum--all for $200... Then we got into a fight and he took them back. I's all ridiculous. But usually I just borrow. Alot of people are very generous in lending me their stuff. If you're careful and respons- ible.
S:What made you decide to learn drums.

L:The great question...Once I said to a friend I have THree reasons. One, I like to sweat. Two, Blondies drummer Clen who is an amazing drummer. I re- ally look up to him. I'd just like to play like that. I had another reason- it's an obscure reason, but whenever I was listening to a song I would sp- eciffically listen to the beat. Of co- urse its the beat that captures you. But it came consious to me... Not just listening to the beat and dancing, but I was ignoring the guit- ars and keyboards and voices and stu- ff. It became extremely consious to me, and I went zing! I just feel there should be more female drummers. If you feel you can handel it.
S:I noticed with your playing that you really keep the beat of the song going. I had the feeling that if you weren't playing the rest of it would fall apart.
L:(Laughter)Yeah, I get that reaction alot.
S:You're also really strong in direc- ting the music, which is something not many drummers do.

L:Oh thank you. (Self-consious, ner- vous laughter). I don't even know if Im consious of that. I don't know. I get real nervous, 'cause I know that whenever we do badley in a song I know that I've done badly. I just automat- ically assume it's me all the way. If the whole song falls apart I know its been me. I can just feel it. But I don't go out there and say...
"I'm gonna direct this song!" I guess it just happens.
S:It's spontaneous...What's going on with the record?
L:Well, good question. As far as the record's concered, it's been sold. To Red Star Records who have expressed extreme intrest in us, but haven't moved their asses. So they bought our single.
S:New blood.
L:Yes. Alot of interest has come, but we get impatient. We intend to work hard enough to get something. We feel we can. It gets very tough,you know. But I have alot of optimistic hopes.
S:So you have a job outside of the band?
L:Not at the moment. 'cause I've got school. I'm in my last year of H.S-- Hi! mom. And so it gets very difficult. I'm looking for one. I need the money.
S:How do you feel when you're playing. Do you think of anything specific?

L:Yes. First of all I think about whats going on. Like I'm listening to the stuff and how and how the songs are going . And then I try and put myself in an objective place. Like, if I was out in the audience and I was listening to this song, what would I think? Would I like it? 'Cause a couple of our songs are like weird! Then of course, I think about the important people who might be out there and what their reactions are.
S:You want commercial success with your music?

L:I guess it would be nice. I'm confused about that stuff, because I'm not quite sure what I want. I'm not quite sure if I want money, or if I just want fame or I just want to play rock and roll all the time--play dru- ms. Or, just be a famous drummer.
S:Are you success oriented?

L:I always wanted to play in a band.. ALways. Always wanted to play drums. I never even considered doing anything else, like singing. (Her sister cuts in:"Except when ya wanted to be a bassoon player...")
L:You know, school music.
S: Is it difficult being so young?

L:Yes. Yes and no. Sometimes it's fun lens are we're young and I guess a litte naive. We feel separated from
the musicians who are 24, 25---who've been playing a long time. The Erasers are all 27, 28--old age land (Laughter) We still get the look ike we're lit- tle kids having fun, who are pretty accomplished for our age. But there'r still seperations. (To Jimmy) Well.. you're old!!
JD:Yeah, but I've made it already.
L:I just come up with a good title for a song and write from that. "The Quake" was written from a personal experience becuase I go to a Quaker school and I was kicked out.
S:Why?

L:Because I was living alone last ye- ar without my parents and they didn't like it. I was living with my bass player, and The Blessed, and half of New York rock was in my apartment. So it was a crazy lifestyle.
S:Talk about your drumming..your sty- le...things like that. What kind of a kit do you want?

L:It's very hard. Maybe a Premier. Maybe a good Pearl set. I dream about having a great drum set Premier would probably be what I'd get. They're very sturdy. One of my problems with player is that my right arm--I play alot of tight beats and it hurts when im playing. I don't get a chance to exercise it enough playing drums because I only have access to a studio once in awhile. When I play, one of my problems is to not get physically or phychologicallly upset about the pain goig through my arm. If I get upset. I start losing the beat. I start getti- ng crazy. So one of my problems is to learn to keep calm and paced.
S:Do you do any kind of exercises?

L:Yeah. Just before I play I take th- e two metal practice sticks and I shake them, keeping the arm straight, as fast as I can. My tendon gets rea- lly sore, but loose. It's also a mat- ter of playing correctly. I can slip into not playing correctly and it can hurt and I start using my arm. One ting I do is keep tha wrist really loose and keep playing with the wrist. That's the only physical problem I have with playing. I have aninsecurity about drumming. People say, "You're really good, one of the best female drummers I've seen. But I'm not happy with myslef yet. I get very insecure about my stle. I have a very simple and straightf- orward style at the moment, because I am not sure how to do other things. I don't wanna get crazy and do ten mil- lion rolls like those rock and roll drummers do. That's a waste. It's ju- st boring.
S:Whose drumming do you like?
L:Well, Ckem Burke is my idol. I also like Chris Frantz (T. Heads-Ed.). Ri- ght now I'm following his style which is very straightforward. There are no female drummers that I know that I like.
S:What are some of your influences?
L:Jimmy. Thank god he's in the shower. He influences me alot. I'm always ar- ound Blondies and their success. I wa-

div.p: A late word from Virgin Records is that Barry Andrews has left XTC to persue a solo career. The band remains together, and the split was said to be amicable.

This interview was done in the dining room of the Gramercy Park Hotel. The resturant was not happy that we were there, and proceeded to make it difficult for us. Barry and I had to repeatedly tell the waiters what we wanted. It made for a bit of an uncomfortable atmosphere. But we survived.
Barry has an extremely dry sense of humor, which was well served admist the frowning waiters.
S:How long have you been playing together?
B:This line-up about two years
S:Where are you from?
B:We're all from Swindon. I was born in London, but moved to Swindon. The others are born and bred
S:Is that near London?

B:It's 80 miles down the motorway. It's an appalling little town known only for railways. I thought you'd know that. It's like a jke in the music papers that we come from Swindon. It's a notoriously un-hip place to come from.
S:Doesn't everyone come from un-hip places and migrate to hip places?
B:Sometimes. That's why we didnt use to cut it with the London music industry, 'cause we were up from the country.
S:Did Did you choose whhat hotel you were going to stay at, or did they just put you here?
B:This is quite good actually, though you wouldn't guess it.
S:This is for the professional hotel person, I think.
B:That's what we are.
S:Do you get tired of being on the road?

B:Yeah, I do. Exept when there's novelty to sustain it, like there is in America, 'cause we've never been here before. Same old clubs, do the same old things night after night can be tiring. It's virtually exhausting.
S:What would you rather do? Would you rather just record and then play certain dates, as opposed to....

B: No, no. I do like gigging when it's done in the right way, I think. But when you just do loads and loads of dates all bound together, on top of each other--which is the only way really you can make it pay, make it pay for itself.....
S:So you wake up and you don't exactly know where you are...
B:You wake up in the night and think youre in a different city..
S:So you do one night stands?
B:Yeah, they're all one night.
S:Youve been doing that for two years?
B:On and off..making albums.
S:DO you like doing that?
B:I like bits of that. All things considered it's not a bad job at all...Beats the shit out of factories.
S:More creativity.
B:To a degree.
S:It seems Brittish bands have less trouble being signed than American bands.
B:There was a big spate of internet around about the time we got signed..They were signing anything that mved the year before last.
S:Did you want to sign?
B:Oh yeah. Anyway we could make money out of it. Enough to live on anyway.
S:Has Virgin treated you well? Given you what you wanted?

B:Always. They're as good as they can be. The only times we have arguments, is when we can't agree between the 4 of us what to do. Then the record company more or less takes over and does the most commerically viable thing they can do under the circumstances.
S:The company is supporting you on this tour?
B:They're paying for it.
S:That's nice of them.
B:Foolhearty of 'em.
S:Have your records done well?
B:No, they've bombed out.
S:How do you feel about that?
B:A bit desperate.
S:Is it bad publicity? Is it that the music isn't accessible for
S:So you think it's only music like the Ramones, which is so blatent, so clear, That people have something to grab on to?
B:Pop music is about that.
S:You define yourself as a pop band

B:Yeah. I don't see us as anything more. I think it's quite a noble call. Being a pop band. (Here I am introduced to Colin Moulding, bass player....Barry comments on
the waiters:"This place is really fascist...")
S:But if all music was Blondie and the Ramones it would be boring. Your music balances that.

B:I don't think it should all be like that. On the other hand, to do that unsuccessfully is a failure, isn't it. And to try and not do that and yet still not come up aith anything atristically valid is a failure as well.
S:You don't want to be a band with a cult following?
B:I don't see any percentage in that at all, although there is a school of thought that courts that.
S:I liked your music because it was visual. It brought to mind really broad ideas. It gave me feelings of things that I'd seen before. Like being in the subway station....Maybe more emotional images.

B:That's good. That's nice to know. If we can only harness this now......I'd really like to be able to so that. To create such strong visual thing so that you could actually depict something and just thrust it upon people. So if you're singing a sing about lonliness, you could actually make the people lonley. That would be great. You can do it roughly, We've done things...Like "Battery Brides". That's super tough. An extent conveys the content. And if you could do that to the power of three.....I could clean up.

S:It seems to me you take melodie apart. Take each sound apart and fit it back together again. Even with the vocals. I wasn't hearing the vocals as words as much as sounds that were fitting together with the rest of the instruments. But you're dealing with an audience which is so conditioned with all kinds of junk music. It's hard for people to discriminate sometimes.

B:You shouldn't need an educated audience. I don't see rock and roll as about having an educated audience anymore than you need to be educated to understand a road accident. It should just be there, and be so spesific, that it's no open to any misinterpretation.
S:I wonder if that's possible. Theres such a difference between what music is out there and what we're allowed to hear.

B:I was thinking about that while getting visas for Canada. Just to be allowed to do that, you've got to tell them all these things. It makes you think of this hugh, gargantuan force that could be turned against you, should you ever really threaten it. They're so powerful they can command you to do this just to be allowed into the country. SO what if you made them really angry?
S:Knock you off.....You all have colds. Did you get them here?
C:Yeah
B:I brought mine over. It's on import. There's harrassment here (from the waiters). Like I'm a criminal.
C:They dont really like us. I mean they do, But not coming in down here (the resturant). They want you to keep in your room.

B:They alwasy stick us in obscure wings. They put us in a hotel in Scarborough once where they were still building it! It's a great hotel; all chandeliers, a golden staircase. The clerk said: "Oh, you're in 148." We go up and up and up and you're in some wing, and the workmen are still in
there! Sawing and hammering.... This is where we get all misty-eyed about our past.
S:How old are you?
C:23. He's 22. Terry's 23 and Andys 25.
S:Are you self-taught musicians?
C:Well, I supposedly had this year of tutoring from this old bloke. He's sort of a bit decrepit, he's like 65. He used teach me songs like "Bill Bailey".
S:Nothing you could use. Did you learn off records?
C:Yeah. He never used to let me turn the amp up. Low volume 'cause the rest of his family were in the other room. It's really inhibiting. I blew that after a year. Couldn't stand the low volume.
S:Do you have a rehearsal studio?
C:WE have a cellar. Our managers' club. Wecan't play too loud because of the Chinese resturant next door.

B:Delicate politics down in the cellar., 'cause you mustn't get in the way of the beer when it comes in. There's nowhere else to practice. That's something about the system that groups need to work on. Rehearsals and early gigs.
S:So what are the crowds like here in comparison to Brittain?
B:Really polite.
S:Do you like that?
B:No, not really. I like the seething mass of pogoers.
S:They wouldn't let you in the front of the stage at CBCG's.
C:The wouldn't?
S:No. They even only let you go one by one to the bathroom down the hall
C:We thought we were all washed up.
B:I hadn't realized that.
S:SO you got the feeling no one liked you?
B:It would be easy to runaway with that impression.
C:I wonder if we could do something about that tonight.
S:There were people behind me beating out the rhythm on my head. They were the seething masses being held behind the reserved seating.
C:I couldn't believe it when the waitress started hanging "Reserved" signs on the tables.
S:Who writes the music?
C:We all do, apart from Terry (drummer). Andy's still the predominant writer. I'm not so far behind.
B:And I'm in the opressed minority.
S:WHat do you want to do? Recording...gigging...
C:Probably not do another album for a hell of a long time. We've done two albums, and I thought we crammed a hell of alot in. I think we can afford to wait.
S:Are you happy with the albums?
C:Yeah.
B:I'm not really. I think the production could have been alot between.
S:Did you pick producers?
B:Yeah. We picked blind really. The mysteries of the 24 track....
C:The thing is we wanted to have our own way. And with a producer like John Lackie it's easy to get your way.

B:But you have to be strong as a producer. What we did with John.......he was the line of least resistance. He let us do what we wanted. He doesn't get in the way, like a fifth member of the group, you know? It's all very polite. And it comes out very polite. You can hear it on both the albums. If you compare that with the live sound.
S:Live sounds alot better.
B:I think it's alot better.
C:Everybody says to me it's alot better. Ninety-five per cent of the people say you're much better live th le say you're much better live than you are on record.
S:You're not talked about as much as Brittish bands like the Clash, Buzzcocks...Is it your music? You're popularity?

B:Part of it's popularity. We're less popular than any of these groups. because we never managed any punk image. Some of them did because they were, & some of them did just to do it. We were pretty naive. We're basically a rock group. That's about it. Therefore we're not affected one way or another by the popularity or unpopularity of new wave people.
S:There are more bands over here that I find similar to you than Brittish bands I can think of.
C:Myabe that's why we're getting accepted over here. I was suprised how popular we've been.
B:Bob Geldorf (Boomtown Rats) ripped us off on a single:"Like Clackwork." He admists he just popped it straight off of us.
S:You don't think immitation is the sincerest form of flattery?

B:Not if he get's all the royalties & we don't. Their are lots of copyists, but none with the same spirit. When we are on stage, There's no one to touch us doing that sort of thing. But on records it's not the same.
S:Have you thought of doing live recordings?
B:Yeah, we;ve thought of that, but it would have to be done in the right way.
S:What kind of music do you listen to?
B:I listen to alot of classical music and reggae, and whatever touches my

But when all the lip {servide} to all these high ideals stops what really matters is the way you run your business. You can be as much of an urban guerrilla as you like on stage. When it really counts is what your ticket prices are, and whether your manager controls it or not.

Laura Davis

Wanna be up there too. I'm influenced by him because I wanna make him proud I wanna get there--where they are. I'm around them alot and the struggles they go through----what they have had to go through to get where they are... It influences me, and gives me more incentive to push harder. They did-- why can't we? I'm pretty optimistic about us. I have alot of faith in the people I play with, 'cause they're so good.
S: You say you see others and it inspires you?

L: But it also scares the living daylights out of me! They go through lawsuits, and they have lawyers and accounts, meetings and offices. It's 1ike a corporation. Very scary. The whole idea, the whole essence, the whole real feeling of the music gets lost somewhere. They're running off to these big meetings around these brown leather labels with lawyers and accountants.... executives from the record company. Where are the songs?
S: Do you think it's possible to avoid that?

L: No. Unless...It's possible to avoid it depending on where you want to go. If you want to go where Blondie wants to go... They want to be rich, so they can't avoid this sort of thing. But if you don't care how much money you get, and you don't care about getting ripped-off by the record company or your manager; you just want to make good music and play, then it's easy to avoid. You just say, "Fuck you" to the meetings, and "Fuck you" to the lawyers and accountants. "I'm writing a song today."
S: Where are you in there?

L: In between. I don't know ‘cause I haven't touched on it yet. With them, it happened very quick. They didn't have time to think about being scared I've seen what happened to them, and if it happens to me maybe I'll know how to deal with it. I'm lucky to be able to see what's going on. It'll be easy when the tine comes, I'll know from watching them what decisions to make.
We haven't really thought of making that our direction. Like we're gonna write this song so we'll be rich. That's why Blondie wrote "Heart of Glass" They wanted to make money.
S: Your songwriting isn't influenced by that?
L: Mainly because we can't write 1ike that, because we don't have the ability. Even 1f we wanted to write a disco tune, I can’t play disco.
S: What about an AM song? Not necessarily disco.
L: There 1s a song, our newest: “Channel 13". I think if it's correctly arranged it can definately be a hit. It would get alot of airplay.

NEW YORK CONTINUES

Vince Scelsa), will not commit itself to the future. WPLJ-FM has sunk to ass-kissing the NY music industry. The surprises are WPIX and WLIB, two stations with a radical difference. PIX carries weekly live recordings of CBGB happenings. Good D.J. 's add to that.

But the best station to listen to has to be WLIB, filling the airwaves with Caribbean music. Reggae and beyond. A place to learn about music that too often ignored elsewhere. Forget Peter Tosh. This is it!
Some stations have Bee Gee boycotts, the flame of resistance in a dismal fog of high voices.
Remember this: New York is always there Every hour at all times with all you can imagine and then some.
On one hand chilling, on the other enlightening. A city full of possibilities. A city of which I never tire. If you haven't: Go There. Stumble in the corners and find the importance.
I remember tall buildings and huge signs and a city bursting at the seams –exploding with the immense. And, I remember color......
MIKI ZONE ZOO/the dots COME ON
Tonight it’s Max's. A chance to see Local luminaries. They come to see the headliner….

But first The Dots. A four-piece young band. Allsion East is one of the best new guitarists I have seen.. She can rock! What a personality! Eyes and mouth wide open; she dances and jerks her hands Spikey hair... like the caucasians in Japanese comics. She is frozen in mid-second as if always surprised.
A great racing guitar sound. Sharp and clean. Good bass

The band's a bit too rock and roll I wish they were more original. Their songs are delivered well, with crispness. lots "Let Me Take You Out To Lunch” stands out. But, they have too many love songs. Nothing new–the male influence?
The singer is not dangerous looking More like deranged. A mad scientist?? He looks and moves furtively. Too much heavy metal music involved…But Allsion is so fresh!
Now for the crowd pleasers…..Miki Zone Zoo (formerly the Fast). They look like an LA Band. Well dressed.. good moves…Flash….
A crisp sound with a look to match. Black and white. Stripes and solids. Taking up the stage like a set sculpture. Even the negative spaces are filled.
MZZ is a band which operates on hyper kinetic energy. Everything is fast. Why wait when we’ll all be gone in a minute? A unit, yet strong individuals pierce through.

The wildest of all is the infamous Miki Zone, guitarist extraordinaire.. With the drummer bashing away at rhythm, the bass player peering out from under long dark bangs, and the singer hopping around like he’s barefoot on
coals, Miki creates the ultimate movement and grips his side of the stage with a wall of force.

A wild player and a visual delight. Miki grimaces, pouts, pounds his head, jumps, hops, spins and camps–all the while playing inspirational guitar. A riveting performer. So slim and dark with clothes almost too big for him: a baggy pin-striped suit with a spider on the lapel.
The singer is wild; Ricky Ricardo with a dash of Valentino. This band’s so obviously having fun!

The hottest number is “The Kids Just Wanna Dance”, better than any shit disco number to get you on your feet. I mean it isn’t just a great song, it’s a tour-de-force for Miki. He takes off his guitar in the middle, hops nonchalantly onto the speaker cabinet, and starts sticking pencils! Yes pencils, into his ears, nose, and mouth.

He takes the pencils one by one and begins to scribble on the guitar strings, as if he’s taking notes. But he is not just screwing around, he really plays! Bounding pencils off the strings, hitting strings for a high staccato sound, playing backwards, upside down. He is manic! What fun he is to see!
This is definitely the most accomplished, the most fun, the most exciting band in New York!

Went to CBGB’s to catch this band. The club is full although the weather stinks. We wade through the crowd to find seats near the wall. You can’t get near the stage here. You gotta sit down. Is this real?

Come On is a young, five-piece band. All are wearing white dress shirts, black pants and white sneakers. Succinct…They look like high school students for the most part, and probably are. Smart & clean.
Their music is a bit reggae, a bit rock, a bit conceptual; experimenting with changes in rhythm and timing.
The lead singer is a good-looking collegiate type kid with horn-rimmed glasses. He sings in a stilted, staccato voice as if he’s having a fit. Pumping his knees; a spastic march in time.

Their guitarist is forgettable. A good rhythm guitar. She reflects the deadpan look of the band. Strong drummer. Their music is Devo-ish, Talking Heads-influenced. Yet originality and humor shine through.

The singer is having artistic spasms.. His face turns red; he sings all the words he can with one breath. You sweat it out with him. His hands in fists, moving like a machine near his body. He pedals like a machine near his body. He pedals with his legs bent at the knees.
The lyrics form a hologram of American blandness. The lyrics are hilarious. Slice-of-life. The singer beats his chest. His hands contorted into fists. An autistic child?
Probably their funniest song is a slap at one of America’s institutions: Disneyland. Like a child wailing at the disappointment of reality:
He delivers it as a tirade; an out-of-breath conversation. Like a victim of reality shock therapy. The best male vocalist I have seen in a while.
At the end he is like an exhausted child. All the tantrums gone. All the visions spent. A band to evoke images of Ladies Home Journal.
It’ll sell in the midwest……

In 1963 I was thirteen. My mom was a country-western singer and I was a farmboy. Also, the Beatles happened… KJR was Radio Free Europe for the refugees out in Duvall. To be honest, it took another year or so for this particular farmkid to catch on to the fact that there was a historic change happening.

When I was in third grade in Sedro Wolley, living next to the movie House where “Love Me Tender” and “King Creole” played, Elvis was my main muse. Dancing in front of mom's stereo to "Hound Dog" and "Don't Be Cruel”.. groovin’ to the Big Bopper, Bobby Darin, Fats Domino and Buddy Holly (the skinny kid with the glasses) on the radio, I had sanction.
Mom took me to hear her sing one Night because I learned the Presley Two-Step (one forward and one back).

But the Beatles, she told me, were awful. Dad watched the Stones on Ed Sullivan with us, and said, “I can see why they’re called dirty. It’s not dirt, it’s Filth!” No sanction. But all the time on my Packard-Bell portable, up in my little room, I was groovin’! To the Folkies. I was enraptured and romanced by Simon’s “I Am A Rock”, and “Young Girls Are Coming To The Canyon” with the Mamas & Papas Dylan, yea. And somehow, when Dylan picked up an electric guitar I wasn’t aware of any outrage. I was down in the barnyard, making those sounds with my mouth.
And I knew those Beatles couldn’t be as awful as mom said. “I Wanna Hold Your Hand” was the Truth to this throbbing pubescent mind.

Unbeknownst to me, the youth, and quite a few of the grown-ups in Seattle, Bellevue, Kirkland were on fire —Rock N Roll was the wave of the future again. And I met them on the traditional meeting ground for city and country: The county fair.

I was in 4-H, of course, and I had a pet Jersey cow to lead around.
Every year we’d go to at least the Monroe county fair and the King County Fair in Enumclaw. Although Enumclaw was the biggest fair, I believe all The hip action was in Monroe.

There was, of course, the rodeo…. horse shows, cow shows, and pie shows Vacuum cleaners, window cleaners, floor cleaners, and organ grinders. But there was also stock car races. And when there weren’t cars on the track the fail officials had found it lucrative to bring half-a-dozen Seattle rock bands to play for free—----there at the racetrack.

Little did they know the ultimate terror they would help bring upon Washington parents everywhere, as their kids became Rock N Rollers, and forgot about doing the dishes and/or feeding the calves. (I noticed they had this much rock n roll only that one year. After that they got all the old country stars they could find).

I must have shoved cow watch onto every kid in the club, so me (I was the president) and Rick DeVries (he’s the vice-president), could go and goggle at Lucky and the Gamblers, the Liverpool Five, and numerous other tatty costumed bands. Everybody looked like Paul Revere and the Raiders… everybody in pseudo-Carnaby Street duds. And Merilee Rush> and the Turnabouts––two shows daily on the midway. I was in love with her overbite.

And there was this scheme which now seems out of a dream. In a tent in some accidental corner of the fairgrounds, kids from Greater Seattle burbs—I swear—were having honest-to-god sanctioned, amateur Battle of the bands. Thirteen year old, sixteen year old Johnny Rays and leather Elvis’s—- tight blue jeans and greasy curls, were climbing onto this little plywood stage with their Fenders and Gibsons and singing “House of the Rising Sun” while their mothers were crawling around in their nylons and Jackie Kennedy coats arranging and checking power cords. What!!??

No kidding. It was like a 4-H club for Rock N Roll. Really, I was out there. I don’t know if they won the chance to be backup band for the Bands at PLU, or if they got to cut a single, or if they just got a new set of strings. But the point is, they were playing rock n roll, and their mothers were not only watching, but brushing their greasy hair before they went on stage. Sanction!

They weren’t as “good”, of course, as the “Professionals” out on the race track; nor did they get the money or attention that Merilee Rush (who would pick up her watch to see how much longer the set was—right in the middle of “Angel Of The Morning”) got… but they felt real-er. They were me, living my dream. They seemed to be not only supported, but even pushed by their mothers to perform and live out that dream.
Sanction.

FROM JET CITY THE NEWS BREAKING THE SOUND BARRIERS

BIRTHS & OBITUARIES
LOCAL RELEASES
SUBHUMANS Death to the Sickoids/Oh Canaduh Crass Productions no label

I like these guys. The A-side is good (although I confess I'm not really sure what Sickoids are), with nice harmonies. The vocals are good, it's hard to find a good male voice in Canaduh. I think this band has potential not fully realized!

While the mix on side two is lousy, the pace is fast and the music is strong. Nice drumming and guitar work, but where is the bass? I think this deserves to be the A-side. It's a great song which could make an anthem for stepped-on Canadians. I can hear Margaret Trudeau humming it now...... "Don't have a job/Can't pay the rent/ And now we're paying interest on the money we've been lent………"
DOA The Prisoner/Thirteen Quintessence Records 1869 W. 4th Ave Vancouver, Canaduh V6J 1M4

One of 2 records on this new label Music from the north. What can I say about DOA? Everybody seems to like them. I have a hard time getting past the vocals. Joey Shithead cannot sing. He cannot even get by with what he does. It's too bad, because the band is good and the music fast. But what the hell is he saying? If it's not important enough to hear, why say it at all? All I could pick out was: "Is everybody a bunch of wimps?" I dunno, Joey. Are you?

The second side suffers from the same problems: lousy vocals. But the drumming of Chuck Biscuits carried the tune along. The only understandable line here is: "I'm one big zero." I think he hit it right on the head.

div.p: THE SHIRKERS Drunk & Disorderly/Suicide Limp Records 1327-J Rockville Pike Rockville, Maryland 20852 I knew the singer Steve Bailer when I lived in D.C. I always thought he was devo, even before I had ever heard of the band. So, I just to get his record… I never would have thought he'd do it. On the whole it's a bit of a disappointment. Too much rock and roll. It's got a good beat, but the overall impact is too soft. I must say I am surprised at how good Steve can sing. Really. I like the female voice on the chorus, it's a nice change. The music is simple. A make-your-own- record-be-a-star project. Capitol city punk without the Capitol city anger.

POINTED STICKS What Do You Want Me To Do/Somebody's Mom Quintessence Records Finally, a great male Canadian singer. It's about time. A perfect pop voice. This is pop! A fun, jumping song! a little boy’s plea with a great beat. This is a tight band all around. The harmonies are good, the hooks are good, and above all the sound is good. A new label with distinction. I think this first song should be on the radio. Pointed Sticks are like the Bay City Rollers with more integrity. A fine debut single from a band worth checking out. You won't be sorry.
Alt text: CUT ME OUT
LEWD Kill Yourself/Trashcan Babies/ Pay or Die Scratch Records 2420 1st Ave Seattle, Wash. 98121

A Clash-like opening. Enemy-like vocals. Can't these guys be original? I guess not. Boring old Satz. I mean, like wow, man this is PUNK! My first question: Why don't You kill yourself Your music is as repetitive as disco.
The second song is a horror. I hate it. Vocal retchings, sexist bullshit. Give up.
The third song. My record player kept rejecting it.
My second question. Do record players have their own tastes in music?
Rita Remark
POLY STYRENE Cont.
POLY: In the new wave I only like the Pistols, apart from us. And Reggae. I was brought up on Reggae 'cause I came from Brixton.
NEVA: Why do you think Reggae has become so popular with punks?

POLY: Well, I like Reggae anyway ‘cause I'm half black, and I grew up in a black area and was brought up on it... So I can’t judge it by what other punks say in any case. But punk and Reggae are the same in the sense that they're basic...Reggae is a very basic music, it's not very technical, the rhythm rules it. It's got its own little language, its own little scene... But it's changed a lot from Ska and Blue Beat, now it's got heavily into Dub and Rastafarian influences. It’s more cultural. There's a lot of fakes in it too, ‘cause if you're a real Rasta you're not meant to show your locks, you keep them under a hat unless you're praying.
NEVA: How old were you when you left home?

POLY: Fifteen. I just moved around for a year, mostly living in squats. I stayed with junkies for a little while. I didn't really like it very much but I didn't have nowhere else to live. There's no flats available for young single people, it's one of the worst problems in London. It's virtually impossible to get somewhere to live, it really is, unless you've got a load of money. These council flats won't let single people in.
NEVA: Why do the papers over here make such a big deal over everything the punks do?

POLY: You know what the English are like! It was just because it was new and exciting that they had to blow it up out of proportion. And it was funny as well, that thing on "Today"- (when the Pistols swore). It brought the fun back into telly, that, and it made the Pistols bloody famous!
NEVA: It sure did. Any last words, Poly?
POLY: Yeah. Do you want a cup of coffee?
page 18
There are many things wrong with the record industry. Any conscious record consumer knows this. But 99% of the record buyers in the world are unconscious.

What this piece amounts to is a bitch session, my personal gripes; laid out in a somewhat random fashion--maybe somewhat carelessly--but the point is clear: There are far too many things being done wrong for one person to change, it is now a matter of raising everyone's level of awareness about the fucked up state of the recording business.

With albums hitting the market at an inflated list price of $8.98 per disc, new groups--the contemporary progressive groups (not progressive in the sense of "techno rock") have a limited chance of making a hit. As record consumers become more and more anesthetized by such high selling, high priced releases as the $12 .98 list Saturday Night Fever, they willingly assimilate the higher priced single LP's. I deny S.N.F.'s existence on its price alone!!!

The high number of sales of a record that retails for at least $8.98 (usually more) shows that people have been irrevocably conditioned to pay astronomical prices for inferior pressings of inferior music. One thing to say for disco listeners is that they openly recognize the inferiority of their music. They openly admit it. "All we wanna do is dance dance, dance."

Most disco records are hot sellers for about two or three weeks, then they are stiffed into oblivion. Some disco records however, employ advanced production techniques. This is good, but actually a technique nicked from the German “psychedelic” musicians of the early and middle seventies: Neu, Cluster, and Kraftwerk.

The disco format has allowed this new music to be presented in a marketable pop format, Some of the recent disco records are almost tantalizing from a production standpoint alone--Donna Summer’s "I Feel Love", for instance. I'd rather have a Nick Lowe or Brian Eno production on any record.

To get back to the point. Consumers are idiots. Do they buy records for the sake of its art, or do they buy it because everyone else does? It is rather difficult to have totally original taste in music. People are hesitant to buy a record they haven't heard before, unless it's by their favorite artist (whether or not that fave lost it five years ago is of no concern). I don't know that many people buy a record based upon reading a review.

The Clash and Lol Creme/Kevin Godley’s "L" have received much critical acclaim, but have sold few albums in this area. Reviews are sometimes "bought" by a record label--either to stimulate sales, or merely to service the press. By exchanging "favors of gratitude" with a writer to do a good review, they buy a sense of security. They're more concerned with radio play. After all, it is where the mass market is.

To change the buying habits of those aillions who bought Fleetwood Mac or Peter Frampton or Saturday Night Fever is like trying to activate a dormant volcano by mortal means. They are comfortable as conformist sheep. To wake them up would shatter their American Dream: Ignorance.

Until then, you can do something. Refuse to buy $8.98 list single albums. Imports are an exception. Their pressing quality is generally superior, and most of the profound music of today is available only in import form.

Artists like Billy Joel, Barbara Streisand, Boston, Steve Miller, Ted Nugent, and Chicago are knowingly allowing their labels to shove their corporate prick up all our asses, Fuck them! Fuck Barbara Streisand and all her "little people” They ought to have the human instinct, alledging themselves to be "artists", to refuse to record and release a record at such prices. They're as openly barbaric as their company presidents and A&R Jerks. It's their profit, as well as

the record company's. Obviously, these types of people are not artists, but profiteers. Modern day carpetbaggers. Hooligan racketeers who tour the world collecting money by the ream. Literally, they're cornholing brown-nosed dick lickers!

This is the situation today. There are plenty of influential musicians who are lucky enough to have Top 100 albums. Of all the new wave artists to release LP's since 1976 (and there are alot of them), only a few have reached a top chart position in the U.S. Patti Smith, Blondie, and the Ramones have all broken through on a limited basis. But consider this: Elvis Costello is the only British new vave artist to be lucky enough to have sold an appreciable number of LP's in the states. Few have actually toured besides Costello, except for scattered dates in the media cities—N.Y., L.A., S.F Cleveland, Detroit, etc.

To wit: Many bands (Clash, Stranglers, Boomtown Rats, Jam, Ultravox, Costello, Generation X, ad infinitum) have been touring Great Britian and Europe for up to three years. Slogging back and forth to small gigs in little towns. But they have support. Possibly because Europe, and England specifically, are more conducive to a greater outgrowth of not only creative impulses, but corporate benevolence.

Throughout history (Gawd! This is sounding heavy!), artists have survived no matter how barely, by receiving grants & benefits from the church, guild, royalty and other wealthy individuals. This feeling is maintained even today. By observing record company signings and promotion activity in Europe, it is easy to see how little risk U.S. record companies are willing to take on a new act, Not another re-working of someone else's broken dreams. Bands like Pink Floyd, Led Zepplin, Fleetwood Mac, Deep Purple, Black Sabbath, ad nauseam, are rarely---if ever---covered by British trade papers. They have completely lost their credibility. They may as well not exist.

Europeans recognize the need to indulge art. It is in their blood. The shit groups mentioned above are still rather large sellers in the U.S., but not in their home countries. They are dead meat. The English rock scene has replenished itself constantly for the last 10-15 years. Good things have been, will and are coming of it. There's been a lot of shit moozik, but a definite mark has been sighted. Industry must bust soon and allow young talent--all the good ones, to make it.
It boils down to that. A total destruction and subsequent restructuring of the whole record industry. And, it is your job (since you bothered to read
this) to do everything in your power to destroy and change it.
To the front!
